answer.rationale: The 18% mandate plus the incumbent's refusal to reopen price effectively forecloses negotiate_terms (memory_c4's mechanism depended on the incumbent being movable) and renew_incumbent (memory_c1/c6 buy stability and volume pricing but not an 18% reduction). memory_c5's defer logic was established on a non-critical renewal with a month-to-month fallback; the primary line at 94% of committed volume with no buffer is not that case, so defer imports a precedent from a materially different risk regime. That leaves the low-cost vendor path, which rests almost entirely on memory_c2 — the single most load-bearing and least corroborated memory here. So memory_c2 is the one to pull: I need the original record to see whether the sharp unit-cost cut and quick onboarding occurred on this component class, at this share of committed volume, and under slack capacity rather than a 94%-utilization, 14-day window. If the source shows the switch was executed with buffer inventory or on a non-constrained part, its transfer to the current situation is weak and I should fall back to a bridged renewal. Given that unresolved dependency, I intend to move primary supply but only as a small guarded test: qualify the low-cost vendor on a limited tranche with the incumbent held as bridge coverage through the expiry, capturing part of the savings without betting continuity on an unverified precedent. memory_c3 supports keeping a second lane live as the delivery-risk hedge. Downstream value risk: memory_c2 records unit cost and invoicing accuracy but says nothing about quality escapes, expedite fees, or service scope — optimizing on the recorded metric could shift cost off the tracked ledger onto line stoppages and rework, and a full switch at 94% utilization would raise delivery risk in direct conflict with the stated objective. I am not treating memory_c2's cost claim as established for this cycle until the archive confirms comparable conditions.
